reflection_text.3:
The deliberation has moved beyond the 25 vs. 26 quorum dispute. The 25 camp’s strongest reply remains that Article I §5 allows a smaller number to compel attendance, so 50 senators plus a friendly VP can eventually pass Article IV statehood legislation despite opposition boycotts. The 26 camp’s strongest point is that quorum is independent of the VP tie-break: 50 senators are not a majority of a full 100-senator Senate, so 25 relies on contested procedural compulsion or at least one opposition senator attending. If quorum compulsion is accepted, 25 still works on the simple arithmetic; if not, 26 becomes the minimum. But this whole 25/26 debate assumes the coalition can instantly have 50 or 52 friendly senators from its states.

The major new issue in round 3 is the staggered Senate election calendar. C6 and C12 argue that the 51-month window from any point in 2000 prevents the coalition from replacing all Senate classes. Worst case is early 2000: only the 2000 and 2002 elections occur before the 51-month deadline, so Class III senators remain potentially hostile. There are 16 states with both Class I and Class II seats, giving 32 guaranteed friendly senators, and 34 states with one of those seats, giving one more each. To get 50 friendly senators (enough with a friendly VP if quorum can be compelled), the coalition needs 16 two-seat states + 18 one-seat states = 34 states. To get 51 friendly senators without relying on compelled attendance, it needs 35 states. If the start is after the 2000 election, replaceable classes are II and III; 17 states have both, so the arithmetic gives 33 states for 50 friendly senators and 34 for 51, but the coalition may not get a friendly President until 2004, leaving very little time. Overall worst case under this election-timing reading is therefore 34 (or 35 if quorum compulsion is rejected).

I find the staggered-election objection legally serious if we do not assume federal senators from coalition states automatically obey the unanimous wish of their state’s People and Government. The problem’s phrase “People (and Governments)” does not obviously bind sitting senators, and there is no recall. The 51-month window seems deliberately short enough to prevent full Senate turnover from early 2000. If this constraint is intended, 25 and 26 are impossible because they cannot produce enough friendly senators within the window. The new leading candidate is 34, with 35 as the fallback if Article I §5 compulsion is deemed too fragile to create quorum. 26 remains viable only if staggered elections are ignored or if senators from coalition states are assumed immediately compliant.

Unresolved issues: whether quorum compulsion is a reliable legal mechanism; whether staggered Senate elections are meant to count; whether the late-2000 start leaves enough time after the 2004 presidential inauguration; and whether DC/Puerto Rico can be coalition members despite not being States for Article V. Current leaning: 34 states under the staggered-election plus compelled-quorum reading; 35 if quorum requires 51 friendly senators; 26 if staggered elections are not considered.

Key mechanics remain: Article IV §3 state-splitting can alter the Article V denominator. With 25 friendly and 25 opposed, splitting friendly states to 75/100 gives exactly 3/4; with 26 and 24 opposed, adding 46 gives 72/96 = 3/4; with 34 and 16 opposed, adding 14 gives 48/64 = 3/4. The bottleneck is controlling Congress enough to pass statehood/splitting legislation, especially the Senate. 24 states cannot control the Senate; 25 gives 50 senators and needs VP tie-break; 26 gives 52 senators and clears quorum/majority without VP; 34/35 arise from Senate election class timing.

The new timing argument: the 51-month window from “any point in 2000” means the coalition cannot assume all its senators are immediately friendly. For an early-2000 start, the deadline falls before the 2004 Senate election, so only 2000 (Class I) and 2002 (Class II) elections are available. There are 16 states with both Class I and II senators, giving 32 senators; the other 34 states can provide at most one senator each. Thus 34 states are needed for 50 friendly senators, and 35 for 51. For a late-2000 start, 2002 (Class II) and 2004 (Class III) are available: 17 states have both, so 33 states suffice for 50 and 34 for 51. A single set of 34 states can be constructed to work for both start scenarios: include all 16 Class I/II states, at least 16 of the 17 Class II/III states, plus others. This makes 34 the minimum if one relies on 50 senators plus VP tie-break and permits quorum compulsion under Article I §5. If quorum requires 51 without compulsion, the minimum rises to 35.

The quorum dispute remains unresolved: Article I §5 requires a majority (51) for quorum, and the VP does not count, but it also allows a smaller number to compel attendance. The 25 camp argues 50 senators can compel one opposition senator, then use VP tie-break; the 26 camp argues 26 is the smallest self-sufficient Senate bloc because it supplies quorum and majority outright. The 26 camp correctly notes that 26 still needs a friendly President to sign statehood bills, so the VP is not a unique external dependency. The 25 camp correctly notes that 26 cannot override a hostile veto with only 52 senators.

The new 34 camp has not fully addressed late-2000 presidential timing: if the wish starts after the 2000 election and the President is hostile, a friendly President may not take office until Jan 2005, leaving only about two months before the 51-month deadline. That may be too tight for statehood plus ratification, though legally possible if everything is pre-planned. The direct Article V route with 38 states avoids President/Congress-control needs but still faces the question whether a hostile Congress can be compelled to call a convention under Article V.

Current leaning: if the puzzle fully incorporates Senate election staggering, 34 is the strongest minimum, with 35 if quorum compulsion is rejected and 38 as a safe direct-Article V fallback. If the puzzle intended to abstract away election timing and individual senator replacement, 25 remains the elegant intended answer, with 26 as the quorum/self-sufficiency alternative. I need to see whether any colleague can show that 34 fails due to the late-2000 two-month window or that the intended reading ignores Senate classes.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m shifting from 26 to **35 States**. C6 and C12 are right that the 25-vs-26 debate is incomplete unless we solve the staggered Senate election problem, but I think C6’s own 34-State answer still leaves a quorum defect, and it is the same defect the 26 camp has been pressing against 25.

In the worst-case early-2000 start, the 51-month window ends before the November 2004 Senate election. Only the 2000 Class I and 2002 Class II seats can be replaced. There are 16 States with both a Class I and Class II seat, so those can supply 2 friendly Senators by 2003. The other 34 States have a Class III Senator plus only one replaceable seat, so they can supply at most 1 friendly Senator.

To get **51 friendly Senators** by 2003, you need all 16 two-seat States, giving 32 Senators, plus 19 one-seat States, giving 19 more. That is \(32+19=51\), so **35 States**.

With 34 States, the maximum is \(32+18=50\) friendly Senators. That is exactly the same 50-Seat trap as the 25-State answer, only shifted into the Senate-class timing. Under Article I, §5, 50 Senators are not a Senate quorum. The Vice President is not a Senator and cannot cure that. If the opposing States simply keep their Senators away, a 34-State coalition cannot organize the Senate or pass the initial Article IV statehood/admission legislation without relying on the attendance-compulsion machinery against hostile Senators. I do not think a “strong coalition” under arbitrary opposition should have to depend on that contested procedural step at the very first Senate hurdle. If we reject 25 because it needs a VP tie-break plus compelled quorum, consistency requires rejecting 34 for needing compelled quorum as well.

With **35 States**, the coalition can actually place **51 friendly Senators** by 2003. That gives both a constitutional quorum and an outright majority, with no VP tie-break and no opposition Senator needed at the first stage. Then the arithmetic works: start with 35 friendly States and 15 opposed States, split friendly States with their legislatures’ consent to add 10 new friendly States, giving \(45/60 = 3/4\) for Article V ratification and well above two-thirds for proposal.

So 34 is a clever near-miss, but it still leaves the coalition one Senator short of being able to constitute a Senate quorum by itself. The smallest robust coalition is **35 States**.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think C6 and C12 are right, and I am updating from 26 to **34 States**. The quorum dispute is now secondary: Article I, §5 does permit a smaller number to compel attendance, so I no longer treat the 50-Senator quorum issue as decisive. But that concession does not rescue 25 or 26, because the harder problem is not attendance—it is the staggered Senate election calendar.

The question says “at any point in the year 2000.” We must handle the worst-case start. If the wish begins early in 2000, 51 months later is around April 2004, before the November 2004 Senate election. So the coalition can influence the 2000 and 2002 Senate elections, but it cannot replace the Class III Senators up in 2004. There are 34 Class III seats. That means only 16 States have both Senate seats replaceable by the deadline; the other 34 States have one Class III seat that remains in hostile hands.

Thus the 25/26 camp’s central assumption—that a coalition of 25 or 26 States immediately supplies 50 or 52 friendly Senators—is not warranted. The existing Class III Senators from those States are not magically converted by the State’s people or government wishing for the amendment. They retain their six-year terms and can be compelled to attend without being compelled to vote yes.

To maximize friendly Senators by the early-2000 deadline, the coalition must include all 16 States with no Class III seat, giving 32 Senators, and then enough one-seat States to reach 50. That requires 18 more States. So the minimum is:

\[
16 \times 2 + 18 \times 1 = 50
\]

and therefore \(16 + 18 = 34\) States. With a friendly Vice President, 50 friendly Senators can pass the initial Article IV statehood/splitting legislation on a tie-break after quorum is obtained. If one insisted on 51 friendly Senators to avoid even compelled attendance, the number would be 35, but under Article I, §5 the compulsion mechanism makes 34 sufficient.

Once the 34-State coalition has passed and signed the statehood/splitting legislation, the arithmetic works cleanly. Start with 34 friendly States and 16 opposed. Add \(x\) new friendly States:

\[
\frac{34+x}{50+x} = \frac{3}{4}
\]

gives \(x=14\). Then there are 48 friendly States out of 64, exactly three-fourths for Article V ratification and well above two-thirds for proposal.

So the real bottleneck is not the VP tie-break and not mere Senate quorum; it is the inability to replace one whole Senate class within 51 months from an early-2000 start. The smallest strong coalition is therefore **34 States**.

**PUBLIC RESPONSE: I remain at 34 States.**

I think the 25/26 debate is still assuming that all Senators from the coalition’s States can be made friendly within the 51-month window. The staggered Senate calendar breaks that assumption.

\[
n + 16 \ge 50 \Rightarrow n \ge 34.
\]

\]

**PUBLIC RESPONSE: I now think the minimum is 34 States.**

The worst case is an early-2000 start: 51 months later is around April 2004, before the November 2004 Senate election. So the coalition cannot replace any Class III Senator. There are 34 Class III seats, meaning only 16 States have no Class III seat.

For a coalition of \(n\) States, the maximum number of friendly Senators it can install by then is:

\[
2(16) + 1(n-16) = n+16
\]

because the 16 no-Class-III States can supply two friendly Senators, while every other included State can supply at most one. To get 50 friendly Senators—enough with a friendly Vice President, assuming Article I §5 allows compelling attendance to obtain quorum—we need:

\[
n+16 \ge 50 \Rightarrow n \ge 34.
\]

reflection_text.4:
Current tentative answer: **34 States**, with **35** as a fallback if Article I §5 attendance-compulsion or the VP tie-break is disallowed. I moved from earlier 25/26 uncertainty to 34.

Decisive new consensus: worst-case early-2000 start means 51 months ends before Nov. 2004 Senate elections, so only Class I (2000) and Class II (2002) seats can be replaced; Class III is locked. In 2000 there are 34 Class III seats, so only **16 States** have both Senate seats replaceable in time. A coalition of \(n\) States can supply at most \(n+16\) friendly Senators by the deadline. Thus:
- 33 States → at most 49 friendly Senators, not enough even with VP.
- 34 States → 50 friendly Senators, enough if 50 can compel quorum under Article I §5 and VP breaks a 50–50 tie.
- 35 States → 51 friendly Senators, self-sufficient quorum/majority if compelled attendance is rejected.

C6’s construction: all 16 Class I+II States, all 17 Class II+III States, plus one Class I+III State = 34; early start gives 50 friendly, late start gives 51. Need to verify it can also control House/Electoral College, but likely possible by choosing populous Class III States. DC/Puerto Rico cannot count initially; they have no voting Senators until admitted.

State-splitting arithmetic: start with 34 friendly, 16 opposed. Add 14 new friendly States via Article IV §3 splitting/consent:
\[
(34+14)/(50+14)=48/64=3/4
\]
for Article V ratification, and 48 > 43 for an Article V convention proposal. Important correction: adding 14 is **not** enough for a congressional 2/3 proposal; use the convention route or add more States.

Remaining disputes:
- C1 still argues 26, assuming coalition States’ Senators are immediately friendly and quorum/tie matters dominate.
- C9 argues 35 because 34 leaves only 50 friendly Senators, not a self-sufficient quorum.
- 34 camp accepts Article I §5 compelled attendance as legal procedural compulsion, not forbidden violence.
- Unresolved: whether compelled attendance is compatible with “no violence”; whether 34 can be chosen to satisfy Senate-class coverage, House control, and 270 electoral votes simultaneously; whether admissions/ratification can be completed within the tight 51-month window.

I lean **34** under the textual Article I §5 reading, with **35** as the stricter fallback.
reflection_text.11:
Round 4 shows a strong shift toward **34 States**. Current tally: 12 colleagues at 34; C1 remains at 26; C9 has moved to 35 because he rejects reliance on Article I §5 attendance-compulsion. My prior leaning was 25 as intended textual answer, 26 as quorum/self-sufficiency alternative, 34/38 as stricter fallbacks. I now lean **34** as the robust minimum under the worst-case timing reading, with **35** only if quorum compulsion or VP tie-break is disallowed, and **38** as a direct Article V fallback.

Key mechanics now central:
- Article V ratification normally needs 3/4 of States: 38 of 50. But Article IV §3 state-splitting/admission can alter the denominator, if the coalition controls Congress/Presidency enough to pass ordinary statehood legislation.
- Senate control is the bottleneck. 25 States = 50 Senators, needing VP tie-break plus quorum compulsion. 26 States = 52 Senators, but the 25/26 debate ignores staggered Senate classes.
- Staggered Senate argument: worst-case start is early 2000; 51 months later is before Nov. 2004. Only 2000 Class I and 2002 Class II elections in time. Class III (34 seats) cannot be replaced. Class counts: I=33, II=33, III=34. State pair types: 16 I/II, 17 II/III, 17 I/III.
- Early-start max friendly Senators from n coalition States is \(2(16)+(n-16)=n+16\) if all 16 I/II States are included. To get 50 friendly Senators: \(n\ge 34\). To get 51: \(n\ge 35\). With 33 States, max is 49, so impossible.
- A 34-State set can work for both early and late starts: all 16 I/II States + all 17 II/III States + one I/III State. Early start gives 50 friendly Senators; late start gives 51.
- Quorum dispute remains unresolved: Article I §5 requires a majority (51) for quorum, but allows a smaller number to compel attendance. Most accept this, so 50 friendly Senators + friendly VP suffice. C9’s 35 argument is that 34 still depends on compelled attendance, same defect as 25. If one rejects compulsion, 35 is consistent.
- Arithmetic: 34 friendly + 16 opposed = 50 States. Add 14 friendly States: \((34+14)/(50+14)=48/64=3/4\), exactly Article V ratification threshold. This also exceeds 2/3 for a convention proposal. C12 noted adding only 14 is not enough for 2/3 of an enlarged Congress, so the proposal must use the Article V convention route or add more States. DC/Puerto Rico can be admitted later but do not reduce the initial Senate bottleneck.
- C1’s counter: if sitting Senators from coalition States can ignore the unanimous State wish, even 34/35 might be defeated by defections. Response: the 34 plan relies on replacing available Class I/II seats to get 50 friendly Senators, not on unreplaceable Class III Senators. Definitional ambiguity remains about how tightly “People and Governments wish” binds their Senators.
- 38 direct Article V route avoids state-splitting but is larger and still faces the question whether a hostile Congress can be forced to call a convention.

Current leaning: **34 States** is the best answer if Article I §5 attendance-compulsion is allowed. Alternative: **35** if quorum must be 51 friendly Senators without compulsion; **26** if the puzzle abstracts away Senate classes; **38** if no state-admission manipulation is allowed. Need watch for any argument that 34 fails due to late-2000 presidential timing or that the intended reading ignores staggered Senate elections.

Thus only the 2000 Class I and 2002 Class II elections occur; Class III senators cannot be replaced. There are 16 States with both Class I and Class II seats, so only those can supply 2 friendly Senators by early 2003; every other included State supplies at most 1. Hence \(n\) States yield at most \(n+16\) friendly Senators. To get 50 friendly Senators—enough with a friendly VP and Article I §5 attendance-compulsion to pass statehood legislation—need \(n \ge 34\). With 33 States, max is 49, which even a VP cannot turn into a majority.

Once in control, add 14 new friendly States: \((34+14)/(50+14)=48/64=3/4\), meeting ratification and exceeding 2/3 for a convention proposal. C12’s correction matters: 14 new States are not enough for congressional proposal by 2/3 of both Houses, so the coalition must use the Article V convention route or admit more States. Initial 34 States already meet the 2/3 convention-application threshold.

Colleague 9 argues for 35 because 34 yields only 50 friendly Senators, and 50 is not a Senate quorum. But Article I §5 and Senate Rule VI appear to allow the smaller number present to compel attendance, so 50 friendly Senators plus a friendly VP should suffice. If compelled attendance/quorum is rejected as too fragile, 35 is the fallback.

DC and Puerto Rico do not reduce the minimum: they are not States for Article V/Senate purposes unless admitted, and admission itself requires the Senate control at issue.

Current leaning: **34 States**, with **35** as a fallback if Article I §5 compulsion is disallowed. reflection_text.2:
Current lean is **34 States**, with **35** as the fallback if Article I §5 attendance-compulsion is disallowed for obtaining a Senate quorum. Round 4 produced a strong shift toward 34: roughly 12 colleagues now support 34 (some with 35 caveat), C1 still holds 26, and C9 moved to 35.

Core basis for 34: the worst-case early-2000 start makes the 51-month deadline fall before the November 2004 Senate election. Thus Class III Senators cannot be replaced. Only 16 States have both Senate seats in Classes I and II; all other States can supply at most one friendly Senator by early 2003. To get 50 friendly Senators—enough to pass Article IV statehood/splitting legislation with a friendly VP tie-break after compelling quorum—requires \(n+16 \ge 50\), so \(n \ge 34\). With 33 States the max is 49, which even a friendly VP cannot save. A 34-State set can be chosen to include all 16 no-Class-III States plus 18 others, and can also be made to control the House and Electoral College.

The initial Senate step: 50 friendly Senators can use Article I §5’s smaller-number attendance-compulsion mechanism to obtain quorum; then a 50–50 vote can be broken by the VP. If that compulsion is rejected, 34 only gives 50, so 51 friendly Senators would be needed, implying 35.

Expansion arithmetic: starting at 34 friendly vs. 16 opposed, adding 14 new friendly States gives \(48/64 = 3/4\), meeting Article V ratification. C12’s correction matters: 14 new States is not enough for 2/3 of an enlarged Congress if proposing by congressional vote, but 34 State legislatures can apply for an Article V convention, or the coalition can add about 25 new States to secure congressional 2/3. So 34 remains sufficient.

The old 25/26 route: 25 gives 50 Senators plus VP tie-break; 26 gives 52 and solves quorum. Both assume coalition Senators are immediately friendly and ignore the staggered Senate calendar. The quorum debate is now secondary; 26 also fails the early-start timing because it cannot produce 50 friendly Senators in time. 25/26 could revive only if one treats the People/Governments’ unanimous wish as automatically binding sitting Senators, which C1 argues; most colleagues reject that under arbitrary opposition.

Unresolved: whether Article I §5 attendance-compulsion is legally acceptable and non-violent enough; whether a late-2000 start leaves too little time after a 2004 election to organize and ratify; whether historical/practical timing prevents admitting and organizing enough new States within 51 months; and whether the direct Article V convention route truly avoids need for congressional cooperation. My position: **34 is best under the worst-case timing reading**, with **35** if compelled quorum is disallowed, and **25/26** only if immediate Senator alignment is assumed.
reflection_text.8:
I now lean **34 States**, with **35 as a caveat** if Article I §5 attendance-compulsion is disallowed or treated as prohibited violence/coercion. This supersedes my earlier 25/26 lean and remains consistent with my prior 34/35 position.

Key persistent points:
- Direct Article V alone requires 38 States to ratify (3/4 of 50); 34 can propose by convention but cannot ratify without enlarging the Union.
- The real route below 38 is Article IV state-splitting/admission: a coalition must first control Congress and the presidency enough to pass statehood/splitting legislation, then add friendly States until 3/4 of the enlarged total are friendly.
- House and Electoral College are not the limiting factor: a chosen 34-State coalition can be populous enough to elect a friendly President/VP and control the House.
- The Senate is the binding bottleneck. Under worst-case early-2000 start, 51 months ends around April 2004, before the Nov. 2004 Senate election. Thus only Class I (2000) and Class II (2002) seats can be replaced; Class III seats (34 seats) cannot.
- In 2000: 33 Class I, 33 Class II, 34 Class III. There are **16 States with both Class I and Class II seats**; 17 with I&III; 17 with II&III.
- For early-start worst case, a coalition of \(n\) States can produce at most \(n+16\) friendly Senators: all 16 I&II States give 32 Senators, and every other included State gives at most 1. Need 50 friendly Senators plus a friendly VP to pass Article IV legislation. \(n=33\) maxes at 49; \(n=34\) reaches 50.
- Quorum: 50 friendly Senators can compel attendance under Article I §5; if all opposition attends, VP breaks 50–50. If compulsion is rejected, need 51 friendly Senators, so \(n=35\).
- Expansion arithmetic: start 34 friendly + 16 opposed; add 14 friendly States by splitting consenting friendly States. Then \(48/64=3/4\) for Article V ratification and \(48/64>2/3\) for a convention proposal. For 35, add 10 → \(45/60=3/4\).
- Proposal: 34 States already exceed 2/3 of 50 for convention applications; after expansion, 48/64 exceeds 2/3. The 14-State addition is not enough for a 2/3 congressional proposal, so use the Article V convention route, or add more States. This is not a fatal correction to the minimum.
- DC/Puerto Rico do not count as States for Article V and do not fix the initial Senate bottleneck; they could be admitted later but do not reduce the initial minimum.
- Current round majority moved to 34; Colleague 9 alone argues 35 on quorum-consistency grounds. The 25/26 camp is now seen as assuming either all coalition-State Senators instantly become friendly or ignoring the staggered Senate calendar. Under an adversarial reading, sitting Senators can remain opposed until their seats are up.

Unresolved/caveats:
- Whether Article I §5 compelled attendance, including possible Sergeant-at-Arms arrest, counts as prohibited “violence.”
- Whether mass state-splitting with no population minimum is fully uncontroversial under Supreme Court precedent.
- Whether Senate filibuster/cloture rules are in play; if so, the minimum would rise above 34/35.
- Whether there is enough practical time from early 2003 to April 2004 to admit/split States, call a convention, and ratify.
- Whether the Article V convention-call duty is fully justiciable if Congress stalls; however, after expansion the coalition likely controls Congress by simple majority anyway.

Current best answer: **34 States**, with **35** if attendance-compulsion is disallowed.
reflection_text.10:
Current lean: **34 States**, with caveat that if compelled Senate attendance is rejected, the answer becomes **35**. The staggered-Senate-election argument is now the decisive bottleneck.

Key points:
- Direct Article V: 34 States to propose by convention, 38 to ratify from 50. DC/Puerto Rico not States for Article V.
- State-splitting/admission route can alter denominator: with Congress/President controlled, split friendly States to reach 3/4 of enlarged total. 34 friendly + 16 opposed, add 14 friendly new States → 48/64 = 3/4; proposal via Article V convention works (48/64 > 2/3). Congressional 2/3 proposal may need more new States, but convention route avoids that.
- Initial bottleneck: must control Senate to pass Article IV statehood/splitting legislation.
- Staggered Senate calendar: worst-case start early 2000 ends ~April 2004, before Nov 2004 election. Only Class I (2000) and Class II (2002) seats replaceable; Class III (34 seats) cannot be replaced in time.
- Senate class overlaps: 16 States with I&II, 17 with I&III, 17 with II&III. Early-start max friendly Senators from n States = n+16. Need 50 friendly Senators + friendly VP (and quorum compulsion) to pass initial statehood bill. n≥34. 33 gives max 49, so fails.
- 34 suffices: choose all 16 I&II States plus 18 one-seat States (e.g., C6 set: all 16 I&II, all 17 II&III, plus one I&III) to get 50 friendly Senators early and 51 late.
- Quorum caveat: 34 early gives exactly 50 friendly Senators. Article I §5 allows a smaller number to compel attendance, so 50 can obtain quorum and then pass with VP tie-break. If this compulsion is disallowed or deemed impermissible coercion, need 35 to get 51 friendly Senators outright.
- C9 argues consistency requires 35 because 34 still depends on compelled quorum; most others accept textual Article I §5 compulsion. C1 remains at 26, arguing coalition States’ own Senators must be counted as friendly; this is the main counter to the calendar argument but seems weaker because Senators are not legally bound by State wishes and may remain opposed until replaced.
- Other unresolved issues: filibuster/cloture if treated as binding would raise threshold; legality/justiciability of aggressive Article IV state-splitting; ability to secure friendly President/VP and House majority with 34 chosen States; timing feasibility from late-2000 start (only ~3 months after 2004 election) but likely assumed manageable if legal steps are available.

Most colleagues now converge on **34**, with **35** only if quorum compulsion is rejected. I find 34 best under a textual reading of Article I §5.
